Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.aspx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ashx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.asmx") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.aspx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ashx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.asmx") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-32201", "CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2026-56164")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-32201", "CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2026-56164")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-32201", "CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2026-56164")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-32201", "CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2026-56164")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js dropper spawns detached 'node -e' child (AsyncAPI Miasma loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the AsyncAPI supply-chain dropper firing at require()-time: a Node.js process spawning a detached background 'node -e'/--eval child to fetch and run the Miasma loader from IPFS. Article-specific because the malicious module executes on module load (no install hook) and immediately launches an inline-eval node child. Rationale: Uses the confirmed behaviour that the dropper fires on require() and launches a detached 'node -e' child (Socket/StepSecurity); node.exe parenting an inline-eval node child is rare in legitimate build workflows and is the earliest host-side signal of the Miasma loader. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit dev tooling that shells out to 'node -e' for quick version/config probes (e.g. some CLI wrappers)
  • Monorepo build scripts using node worker bootstrapping via -e
  • Test runners spawning node with --eval snippets
  • Electron/CI helper scripts invoking node -e for env detection
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest", "mocha", "electron-builder", "semantic-release") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the node -e child and decode any inline/base64 payload; check whether the parent node process was inside a project that installed @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1, generator-components@0.7.1 or specs 6.11.2. 2) Contain: isolate the host and revoke developer credentials (npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH) reachable from it — the payload harvests these. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for outbound IPFS traffic (85.137.53.71, ipfs.io CID) and sync.js file writes, and search other endpoints that resolved the affected package versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e ", " -e\"", "--eval", " -e '")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (" -e ", "--eval")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound C2 to Miasma IPFS gateway / 85.137.53.71 from Node.js AICommand & Control Medium
Detects egress to the AsyncAPI/Miasma second-stage infrastructure: the hardcoded C2 IP 85.137.53.71 (any process) and the IPFS gateway path carrying CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9, especially when initiated by node.exe. Article-specific because these are the exact download and REST-C2 endpoints named by the researchers. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 and the IPFS CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 are hard IOCs confirmed by OX Security, Socket and the article's own IOC list; the IP is a fixed-string match so FP rate is near-zero, and node/npm reaching a public IPFS gateway is itself anomalous on build hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/ • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate projects that genuinely pin dependencies or assets on ipfs.io (rare on corporate build hosts)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the sample and reaching the same IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment scanners re-resolving the CID
  • A researcher manually curling the IOC during investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which local process initiated the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether the host imported an affected @asyncapi version; the CID hit means the second-stage was actually pulled. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 and the CID at proxy/egress, isolate the host, and rotate all developer secrets on it. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for any host that resolved ipfs.io from node/npm in the last 30 days and for the 'node -e' spawn pattern and sync.js drops.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
    or RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
    or (RemoteUrl has "ipfs.io" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
    or Url has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
    or Url has "ipfs.io"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma 'sync.js' loader written by Node.js or known-bad AsyncAPI payload hash AIInstallation Medium
Detects the encrypted second-stage 'sync.js' loader being written to OS-specific paths by a node process, or any file matching the seven published AsyncAPI/Miasma payload SHA256 hashes. Article-specific: sync.js is the named loader dropped after the IPFS fetch. Rationale: 'sync.js' is the named loader and the seven SHA256 values are the published payload hashes (Socket/SafeDep/OX IOC lists); a node process writing sync.js or any file matching those hashes is a definitive install-stage indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-ASYNCAPIGENERATOR-14103255
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate projects that ship a benign 'sync.js' module built by a node bundler (name collision — hash filter disambiguates)
  • Webpack/rollup emitting a chunk named sync.js into dist/
  • node writing sync.js into node_modules during a legitimate install of an unrelated package
  • Editor/formatter rewriting a source file literally named sync.js
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\dist\", @"\build\", @"\.next\") and SHA256 !in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1","082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab","bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4","9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b","d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7","6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71","9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if a SHA256 matched, treat as confirmed; if only the sync.js+node heuristic fired, hash the file and compare to the seven IOCs and inspect for encrypted/obfuscated blobs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node processes, remove the dropped loader and any autostart entries, and rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with the 'node -e' spawn and IPFS/85.137.53.71 egress on the same host, and check systemd/cron/launchd/Run-key persistence.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "sync.js" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe"))
    or SHA256 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1","082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab","bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4","9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b","d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7","6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71","9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where (TargetFileName =~ "sync.js" and ActingProcessName has "node")

Node.js writes Windows Run-key autostart pointing at .js/node (Miasma persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Miasma persistence step on Windows: a node/npm process writing a CurrentVersion\Run autostart value whose data references node or a .js loader (e.g. sync.js). Article-specific because Miasma sets up its own autostart across systemd/crontab/launchd/Windows Registry, and a node process authoring a Run key is highly abnormal. Rationale: Miasma's own persistence (Windows Registry autostart) is confirmed by the article and Socket; a node/npm binary authoring a Run key is behaviourally abnormal (node is a build tool, not a persistence author), giving high fidelity even without a fixed value string. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/ • https://gbhackers.com/miasma-worm-returns-as-rat/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based installers (e.g. some Electron app setups) that legitimately register a Run key for their own app
  • nvm/volta or dev-environment managers writing startup shims
  • A packaged CLI that adds itself to autostart on first run
  • Enterprise deployment scripts wrapping node to set startup entries
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any ("AppData\\Local\\Programs\\", "\\Electron\\") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--squirrel")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — if it points at a .js under a temp/user path or references sync.js/node -e, treat as malicious; confirm whether the host imported an affected @asyncapi version. 2) Contain: delete the Run value, isolate the host, kill persistent node processes, and rotate developer secrets. 3) Hunt: check the same host for sync.js drops, IPFS/85.137.53.71 egress and the node→node -e spawn; on macOS/Linux dev hosts check launchd plists, crontab and systemd user units created by node.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"CurrentVersion\Run"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe")
    or RegistryValueData has_any ("node", "sync.js", ".js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"CurrentVersion\Run"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR *\CurrentVersion\run\*) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\npx.exe)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/CurrentVersion\\Run/i ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|npx)\.exe$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:

            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

status: experimental
description: |

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

let BadHashes = dynamic(["34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

let LookbackDays = 7d;

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256

| order by files desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF via /wsproxy websocket upgrade to external host (CVE-2026-15409) · [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 AMC hotfix rollback with path-traversal name (CVE-2026-15410 code injection)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 backdoor endpoint /__api__/login|logout returning HTTP 200 (post-exploit) · [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 NGINX Unit conf.json backdoor route persistence (/__api__/login|logout) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Two SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days Exploited, One Could Enable Admin Commands
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF via /wsproxy websocket upgrade to external host (CVE-2026-15409) AIExploitation High
Hunts SonicWall SMA 1000 web access logs for requests to the /wsproxy endpoint carrying a suspicious host parameter that return HTTP 101 (WebSocket switching-protocols), the exact forensic indicator SonicWall published for unauthenticated SSRF exploitation of CVE-2026-15409. Article-specific because /wsproxy proxying to an attacker-chosen host with a 101 upgrade is the concrete SSRF footprint, not a generic proxy hit. Rationale: Uses SonicWall's own published IoC (requests to /wsproxy with suspicious host parameters returning HTTP 101 in extraweb_access.log) — an exact string+status pair, high fidelity because legitimate SMA config uses named bookmarks not arbitrary host params. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Work Place WebSocket tunnels to sanctioned internal RDP/SSH/VNC bookmarks that also return 101
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health checks probing /wsproxy
  • Penetration testers or vulnerability scanners validating the patch post-remediation
  • Administrator functional testing of tunneled applications after an upgrade
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full extraweb_access.log entry — extract the host/target parameter passed to /wsproxy and confirm it is an unexpected/external destination rather than a provisioned bookmark; note the source IP and User-Agent. Step 2 (contain): If the target is attacker-controlled, isolate the appliance from untrusted networks, block the source IP at the perimeter, and confirm the appliance is on 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835 or higher — if not, patch immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Follow SonicWall guidance — re-image physical or redeploy virtual appliances if compromise confirmed, then rotate all user/admin passwords and reset TOTP tokens; pivot to the /__api__ and ctrl-service.log indicators to check for follow-on code injection.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/wsproxy"
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"\s101\s"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF via /wsproxy WebSocket Upgrade (CVE-2026-15409)
id: 8f2a4c11-6b3d-4e7a-9c21-2d5e7f8a1b90
status: experimental
description: Detects requests to the SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy endpoint returning HTTP 101, the published forensic indicator of unauthenticated SSRF exploitation.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/two-sonicwall-sma-1000-zero-days.html
  - https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1090
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/wsproxy'
    sc-status: 101
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate SMA portal WebSocket tunnels to known internal RDP/VNC/SSH bookmarks
level: high
source:linux.syslog "/wsproxy" "101"
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

SonicWall SMA 1000 backdoor endpoint /__api__/login|logout returning HTTP 200 (post-exploit) AIInstallation High
Hunts SonicWall SMA extraweb_access.log for requests to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout that return HTTP 200. SonicWall states these URIs do not exist in legitimate configuration, so any 200 response is a high-fidelity indicator that an attacker has injected a rogue NGINX Unit route to gain a foothold after chaining the SSRF and AMC code-injection flaws. Rationale: SonicWall explicitly states /__api__/login and /__api__/logout do not exist in legitimate config; a 200 response is therefore an attacker-injected route — a near-zero-FP forensic IoC directly from the vendor advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vendor/IR forensic tooling replaying the IoC against the appliance during an investigation
  • Vulnerability scanner signature that probes these exact paths and the appliance echoes a 200 error page
  • Custom SonicWall support script deliberately hitting the URI to validate patch state
  • Non-SonicWall device sharing the same syslog index that legitimately serves an /__api__ path
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the 200 response actually originated from the SMA appliance (not another host in the syslog pool) and capture the source IP, session cookie, and User-Agent. Step 2 (contain): Treat the appliance as compromised — isolate it, block the source IP, and per SonicWall re-image physical or redeploy virtual appliances; do NOT simply delete the route. Step 3 (hunt): Inspect /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the injected route, review ctrl-service.log for hotfix-rollback path-traversal entries, then rotate all user and administrator passwords and reset TOTP tokens.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"\s200\s"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 AMC hotfix rollback with path-traversal name (CVE-2026-15410 code injection) AIExploitation High
Hunts ctrl-service.log for hotfix rollback operations whose names contain path-traversal sequences (../), the SonicWall-published indicator that the post-authentication AMC code-injection flaw CVE-2026-15410 was used to run arbitrary OS commands as administrator. Article-specific because it keys on the abnormal rollback filename shape, not generic upgrade activity. Rationale: Keys on SonicWall's published indicator 'hotfix rollbacks with path traversal names' in ctrl-service.log — a legitimate rollback name never contains '..', making the traversal sequence the high-fidelity discriminator for CVE-2026-15410 command injection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-issues-urgent-sma-patch-warning-for-two-zero-day-exploits/
ATT&CKT1059 T1083 T1211
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator performing a legitimate, supported hotfix downgrade (rollback name is a clean version string, no '..')
  • SonicWall support-directed troubleshooting that manipulates hotfix state
  • Log line quoting a file path that incidentally contains '..' in an unrelated context
  • Backup/restore tooling replaying historic ctrl-service.log entries into the SIEM
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the full rollback target string from ctrl-service.log and confirm it contains a traversal sequence pointing outside the hotfix directory rather than a normal version identifier; correlate the timestamp against admin AMC logins. Step 2 (contain): Assume administrator-level OS command execution — isolate the appliance, and per SonicWall re-image physical or redeploy virtual appliances; verify version is 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835+. Step 3 (hunt): Review /var/lib/unit/conf.json for rogue /__api__ routes and extraweb_access.log for the SSRF (/wsproxy 101) and backdoor (/__api__ 200) indicators, then rotate all credentials and reset TOTP tokens.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "ctrl-service" or ProcessName has "ctrl-service"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("hotfix", "rollback")
| where SyslogMessage has ".."
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 NGINX Unit conf.json backdoor route persistence (/__api__/login|logout) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the presence of /__api__/login or /__api__/logout route definitions inside the SonicWall SMA NGINX Unit config (/var/lib/unit/conf.json), or config-reload log lines referencing them. SonicWall states these routes do not exist in legitimate configuration, so their appearance in conf.json is a durable backdoor/persistence indicator planted via the CVE-2026-15410 code-injection flaw. Rationale: Directly implements SonicWall's forensic check that /var/lib/unit/conf.json must not contain routes for /__api__/login or /__api__/logout — presence is an attacker-planted persistent route, a durable host-based IoC distinct from the transient access-log hits. SonicWall SMA1000 SSRF: phantom /__api__/login|logout (HTTP 200) and /wsproxy (HTTP 101) requests AIExploitation High
Hunts the initial-access footprint of CVE-2026-15409 exploitation on SMA1000 appliances: requests to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout that return HTTP 200, and /wsproxy websocket upgrades returning HTTP 101. SonicWall states these URIs do not exist on a clean appliance, so any successful hit is a compromise indicator, not benign traffic. Rationale: Uses the vendor-confirmed non-existent URIs /__api__/login, /__api__/logout (HTTP 200) and /wsproxy (HTTP 101 websocket upgrade) from the SonicWall advisory - any successful response is high-fidelity because these paths are absent from legitimate SMA1000 configurations. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sonicwall-sma1000-0-day-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1090.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or vulnerability scan of the appliance deliberately probing these URIs (would still be a real 200/101 - correlate with change-management ticket)
  • A misconfigured upstream load balancer or reverse proxy rewriting health-check paths onto /wsproxy
  • Log-parser mis-extracting the status code from a non-standard access-log format, producing false 200/101 values
  • Replayed archived logs from a previously-compromised appliance being re-ingested
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and that the appliance is a genuinely unpatched SMA1000 (below 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835). Pull the full extraweb_access.log lines around the hit to see the sequence of /__api__/* and /wsproxy calls. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the appliance from the internet (block WAN mgmt/Work Place access), and begin the vendor-mandated response - re-image physical or redeploy virtual appliance, since these flaws have no workaround. Step 3 (hunt): Check /var/lib/unit/conf.json for injected /__api__ routes and ctrl-service.log for path-traversal hotfix rollbacks; rotate all user/admin passwords and reset TOTP tokens.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout", "/wsproxy")
| extend ReqUri = extract(@'"[A-Z]+\s+(\S+)\s+HTTP', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend HttpStatus = toint(extract(@'HTTP/\d\.\d"?\s+(\d{3})', 1, SyslogMessage))
| where (ReqUri in ("/__api__/login","/__api__/logout") and HttpStatus == 200)
    or (ReqUri startswith "/wsproxy" and HttpStatus == 101)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ReqUri, HttpStatus, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA1000 backdoor: rogue /__api__/login|logout routes injected into NGINX Unit conf.json AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence artifact from SMA1000 compromise: rogue HTTP route definitions for /__api__/login or /__api__/logout written into the NGINX Unit configuration at /var/lib/unit/conf.json. SonicWall confirms these route URIs never appear in a legitimate appliance config, so their presence in the config file is a durable-backdoor indicator. Rationale: Pins on the vendor IOC that /var/lib/unit/conf.json containing /__api__/login or /__api__/logout routes is illegitimate; combining the exact config path with the never-legitimate route strings makes this a low-FP persistence indicator. Telemetry depends on the appliance forwarding config/auditd events, so it is a hunt where FIM is present. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall hotfix/patch install rewriting conf.json (would NOT add /__api__/login|logout routes - the route strings are the discriminator)
  • Vendor support session regenerating the Unit config during troubleshooting
  • Backup/restore of the appliance config replaying an older conf.json into logs
  • Config-diff tooling echoing the full conf.json (including the malicious routes) into an audit log after the appliance was already flagged
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve /var/lib/unit/conf.json from the appliance and confirm a route block referencing /__api__/login or /__api__/logout exists - these are never present in a clean config. Cross-check timestamps against extraweb_access.log SSRF hits and ctrl-service.log rollbacks. Step 2 (contain): Treat the appliance as fully compromised - take it offline, then re-image (physical) or redeploy (virtual) per SonicWall guidance; do not attempt to hand-edit conf.json. Step 3 (hunt): Reset all user and admin passwords and TOTP tokens, review VPN session logs for external admin logons, and sweep other appliances in the fleet for the same conf.json routes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/var/lib/unit/conf.json"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA1000 code injection: hotfix rollback with path-traversal artifact names in ctrl-service.log AIExploitation High
Hunts CVE-2026-15410 post-auth OS-command execution on SMA1000: the code-injection flaw manifests as hotfix-rollback operations in ctrl-service.log whose target/artifact names contain path-traversal sequences (../). Legitimate rollbacks never reference traversal paths, so these entries evidence both arbitrary command execution and hotfix-downgrade defense evasion. Rationale: Combines the vendor IOC 'hotfix rollbacks with path traversal names in ctrl-service.log' - the rollback keyword plus a ../ traversal sequence is the observable signature of CVE-2026-15410 command injection, and legitimate rollbacks never carry traversal artifact names, keeping FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sonicwall-sma1000-0-day-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine SonicWall hotfix rollback during supported downgrade (references a normal versioned artifact name, no ../ sequence)
  • A log line quoting a user-supplied filename that innocently contains .. (rare in ctrl-service context)
  • Automated patch tooling logging relative paths that resolve within the intended directory
  • Re-ingested historical ctrl-service.log from an appliance already known-compromised
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has "rollback" and SyslogMessage has_any ("12.4.3-03453","12.5.0-02835") and not (SyslogMessage has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c")))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the offending ctrl-service.log lines and confirm the rollback target/artifact name contains a ../ (or encoded) traversal sequence and correlate the timestamp with any /__api__ SSRF hits and conf.json changes. Verify the appliance hotfix version was downgraded to a vulnerable release. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the appliance and initiate re-image/redeploy - a traversal rollback means arbitrary command execution occurred and the appliance state cannot be trusted. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all commands run around the rollback, review admin console auth for the account that authenticated (CVE-2026-15410 is post-auth), rotate credentials/TOTP, and check the fleet for the same rollback pattern.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has "ctrl-service" or SyslogMessage has "ctrl-service" or SyslogMessage has "hotfix"
| where SyslogMessage has "rollback"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%5c", @"..\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "rollback" ("hotfix" OR "ctrl-service") ("../" OR "..%2f" OR "..%5c")
APPLICATION
index=* (source="*ctrl-service.log*" OR TERM(ctrl-service)) TERM(rollback) ("../" OR "..%2f" OR "..%5c" OR "..\\")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample_events by host source
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

FacturaScripts traversal file-write: web-server drops PHP/.htaccess into Dinamic/Assets or node_modules AIExploitation High
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-write primitive of GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4: the FacturaScripts web-server process writing a file with a dangerous extension (php-family, .htaccess, .txt, .html) into the Apache-direct-served Dinamic/Assets/ or node_modules/ directories, which normally only ever hold shipped JS/CSS/images and npm packages. Uploaded content is supposed to land only in MyFiles/, so any such write outside it via UploadedFile::move() is the traversal itself. Rationale: Uses the article's exact write targets (Dinamic/Assets/, node_modules/) combined with the file extensions the isValid() blocklist fails to stop (.htaccess, .txt, .html and, via disguise, php-family) — a web-server process writing these into shipped static dirs is the traversal itself, since legitimate uploads only ever go to MyFiles/. Cross-checked against the FacturaScripts upload-RCE advisory family. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Plugin install/update where FacturaScripts regenerates Dinamic/ classes and compiled assets
  • Composer or npm writing legitimate packages into node_modules during a deployment
  • Theme/asset build tooling emitting README.txt or .html docs under an assets folder
  • Backup/restore of the application directory re-creating files as the web-server user
  • Admin manually copying files into the web root as www-data
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("composer","composer.phar","npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe","git","git.exe","php") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","deploy","ci")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the writing process is the live web-server user (www-data/apache) and NOT a deploy pipeline (composer/npm/git); inspect the written file's content — PHP tags, `AddType`, or an obfuscated blob = confirmed. Note source IP from the app/access logs at that timestamp. Step 2 (contain): Delete the dropped file(s), revoke the API token / session used, and add a `Deny from all` rule (or WAF block) on /Dinamic/Assets/ and /node_modules/ dynamic content. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all files under Dinamic/Assets and node_modules by mtime for other drops, look for a paired `.htaccess`, and pivot on the source IP across the upload endpoints /api/3/uploadfiles and /api/3/attachedfiles.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe","nginx.exe","nginx")
| where FolderPath contains "Dinamic/Assets" or FolderPath contains @"Dinamic\Assets" or FolderPath contains "node_modules"
| extend FileExt = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
| where FileName =~ ".htaccess" or FileExt in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","txt","html","htm","shtml")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","php","nginx","w3wp")
| where TargetFilePath contains "Dinamic/Assets" or TargetFilePath contains @"Dinamic\Assets" or TargetFilePath contains "node_modules"
| extend FileExt = tolower(tostring(split(TargetFileName, ".")[-1]))
| where TargetFileName =~ ".htaccess" or FileExt in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","txt","html","htm","shtml")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts .htaccess PHP-handler remap dropped into Dinamic/Assets (RCE enabler) AIInstallation High
Hunts Step 3 of the GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 chain: an .htaccess written by the web-server process into the rewrite-excluded, Apache-direct-served Dinamic/Assets/ (or node_modules/) directory. Attackers drop `AddType application/x-httpd-php .png` there so a follow-up benign-extension upload executes as PHP. A runtime-written .htaccess in these directories is a near-unambiguous RCE-staging signal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise RCE-staging action — a runtime-written .htaccess in the rewrite-excluded Dinamic/Assets/ dir (needed because that path bypasses index.php and .htaccess is missing from BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS). This is a single, high-fidelity indicator with essentially no benign runtime cause. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Puppet) deploying .htaccess as the web-server user during a release
  • Manual admin hardening that places a Deny-all .htaccess (though the recommended fix targets MyFiles/, not Dinamic/Assets/)
  • Plugin installer that legitimately ships an .htaccess inside its asset payload
  • Application self-heal routine regenerating Dinamic/ during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","composer","git") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","deploy","ci")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the .htaccess content immediately — presence of `AddType`, `SetHandler application/x-httpd-php`, or `php_value` = confirmed RCE staging. Correlate timestamp with a preceding write into the same directory (the payload). Step 2 (contain): Delete the .htaccess and any paired payload, kill the php-fpm workers if a web shell is suspected, revoke the offending API token/session, and block the source IP. Step 3 (hunt): Search web access logs for GETs to files under /Dinamic/Assets/ served with a 200 shortly after; grep the directory for files containing `<?php`; verify the patched UploadedFile::move() applies basename() and that htaccess is now in BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".htaccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe","nginx.exe","nginx")
| where FolderPath contains "Dinamic/Assets" or FolderPath contains @"Dinamic\Assets" or FolderPath contains "node_modules"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ ".htaccess"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","php","nginx","w3wp")
| where TargetFilePath contains "Dinamic/Assets" or TargetFilePath contains @"Dinamic\Assets" or TargetFilePath contains "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts traversal payload retrieval: HTTP GET for non-static file under /Dinamic/Assets/ or /node_modules/ AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the retrieval/execution stage of GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4: an inbound GET for a PHP-family, .txt or .htaccess file directly under /Dinamic/Assets/ or /node_modules/, which Apache serves without going through index.php. These directories normally return only JS/CSS/fonts/images, so a request for a script or text file there indicates an attacker fetching a traversal-dropped payload or web shell. Rationale: Targets the article's reachable-payload URLs (https://target/Dinamic/Assets/x.png|traversed.txt) using the fact that the shipped htaccess-sample excludes /Dinamic/Assets/ and /node_modules/ from the index.php rewrite, so a script/text-file GET there is served directly and is anomalous. Kept as hunting because png-disguised payloads and rare legit .txt readmes limit fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate readme.txt / license.txt shipped inside a node_modules package being fetched
  • Vulnerability scanners or pentest tools probing common web-shell paths
  • Uptime/monitoring bots requesting asset paths
  • A plugin that legitimately serves a .txt data file from its assets folder
  • Search-engine crawlers indexing exposed asset directories
Suppression filter
| where not (csUserAgent has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Pingdom") ) | where not (UriLower endswith ".txt" and csUriStem contains "/node_modules/" and csUriStem has_any ("readme","license","changelog"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each hit, check scStatus — a 200 on a .php/.phtml under /Dinamic/Assets/ means the handler executed; pull the response size and the source IP's prior POST to /api/3/uploadfiles or /api/3/attachedfiles. Step 2 (contain): Remove the served file, block the source IP, and disable direct serving of these directories (WAF rule or Apache Require all denied). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the source IP back to the file-write and .htaccess UCs on the host, review authenticated sessions/API tokens from that IP, and confirm the UploadedFile::move() basename() patch is deployed.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem contains "/Dinamic/Assets/" or csUriStem contains "/node_modules/"
| extend UriLower = tolower(csUriStem)

Critical

Coordinated AsyncAPI Supply Chain Attack: Miasma RAT Delivered via Compromised CI/CD Pipelines in Two Repositories

StepSecurity
2026-07-14 15 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 14, 2026 at 07:10 UTC, three packages in the AsyncAPI generator monorepo (@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, and @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1) were published to npm carrying an obfuscated dropper that fires the moment the library is loaded, not on install. The packages were published through the project's own legitimate GitHub Actions release workflow and carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations, because the attacker didn't steal an npm token: they gained push access to the repository's next branch and let the project's real CI/CD pipeline do the …

Miasma RAT C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 from Node.js runtime AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the StepSecurity/Harden-Runner-confirmed Miasma HTTP C2 endpoint 85.137.53.71 (three ports) originating from a Node.js process after a compromised @asyncapi package is loaded. Article-specific because the dropper fires on library load and beacons to this exact confirmed IP. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is StepSecurity/Harden-Runner-confirmed (observed egress directly) and cross-verified by Socket.dev and Safedep as the Miasma HTTP C2 on three ports; any host contacting it is a confirmed compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer VPN/proxy egressing through an IP that happens to overlap after reassignment (verify WHOIS ownership before closing)
  • Threat-intel sandbox or research VM intentionally detonating the sample
  • Security scanner validating IOC reachability from a jump host
  • Shared NAT gateway masking which internal host actually beaconed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src host and the initiating process (expect node.exe); pull the full process tree and the loaded @asyncapi package version. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 85.137.53.71 at egress on all three ports, and kill the node process; rotate any developer secrets on that host (npm/GitHub/AWS tokens, SSH keys) as Miasma is a credential stealer. 3) Hunt: sweep for other hosts contacting 85.137.53.71 or resolving the fallback channels, and inventory all machines with the malicious @asyncapi versions installed.

| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js resolving Miasma fallback C2 channels (BitTorrent DHT / Nostr relays) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution / connections from a Node.js process to Miasma's fallback dead-drop resolver infrastructure — router.bittorrent.com, dht.transmissionbt.com, relay.damus.io, relay.nostr.com — used when the primary HTTP C2 is unavailable. Legit Node apps almost never touch BitTorrent DHT bootstrap or Nostr relays. Rationale: Harden-Runner directly observed router.bittorrent.com and dht.transmissionbt.com egress; Socket.dev and Safedep confirm Nostr relays (relay.damus.io/relay.nostr.com) and BitTorrent DHT as documented Miasma fallback channels — a Node.js process touching these is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a legitimate BitTorrent/IPFS/libp2p Node application on a workstation
  • A Nostr client or decentralized-app project being built/tested locally
  • P2P-based package mirror or content-distribution tooling
  • Security researcher replaying the sample in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webtorrent","ipfs-desktop","nostr-tools") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node.exe and correlate with the @asyncapi package load; check whether the same host also hit 85.137.53.71. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the four fallback domains at DNS/egress, kill node, and rotate developer credentials on the box. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts querying these domains from node, and check CI/CD build agents which are the highest-value Miasma targets.

Detached 'node -e' launcher downloading Miasma second stage from IPFS AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma launcher pattern: a Node.js process spawning a hidden/detached child 'node -e' that pulls sync.js from an IPFS gateway. The command line carries IPFS/sync.js/NodeJS markers, distinguishing it from benign node -e build helpers. Rationale: Socket.dev and Safedep both document the launcher spawning a detached 'node -e' child that downloads sync.js from an IPFS gateway into a hidden NodeJS directory; node-parenting-node with -e plus IPFS/sync.js markers is the article-specific execution fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling that legitimately shells out to node -e for a quick eval (e.g. version print)
  • A developer manually using an IPFS Node library (js-ipfs / helia) for legitimate work
  • Electron/desktop apps that self-spawn node -e helper processes
  • Postinstall scripts of unrelated packages invoking node -e
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("console.log(process.version)","--version") and ProcessCommandLine !has "ipfs")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full -e payload string and decode the IPFS CID/gateway URL; confirm the parent is a build/CI or dev-tool node process loading @asyncapi. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill both node processes, remove the dropped NodeJS\sync.js, and block the C2/fallback infra; rotate secrets on the host. 3) Hunt: search for the same node->node -e chain org-wide and for sync.js drops (see companion file-drop UC).

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-e"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs","sync.js","NodeJS")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Miasma sync.js payload dropped to hidden 'NodeJS' directory AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second-stage write: sync.js landing in the OS-specific hidden 'NodeJS' directory under a user profile, or a file matching the known Miasma dropper hashes. This is the on-disk staging step the launcher performs before spawning the detached RAT. Rationale: All four write-ups (StepSecurity, Socket.dev, Safedep, JFrog) describe the payload dropping sync.js into an OS-specific hidden 'NodeJS' directory; the filename+path and the article's three SHA256 dropper hashes make this a precise on-disk anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app that happens to create a user-profile 'NodeJS' folder with an unrelated sync.js (rare)
  • Corporate software distributing a signed sync.js helper
  • Backup/EDR agents touching the file during scan (initiating process would not be node.exe)
  • Developer manually placing a sync.js script in a NodeJS-named workspace
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or isnotempty(SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe and hash the dropped sync.js against the three known IOCs; determine which @asyncapi package triggered it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine/delete NodeJS\sync.js, kill the detached node process, and rotate developer secrets. 3) Hunt: submit the sample hash to the fleet, sweep all hosts for the hidden NodeJS\sync.js path, and correlate with C2 beacons to 85.137.53.71.

  • A researcher or IR team intentionally reproducing the compromise in a sandbox
  • Internal mirror/cache scan enumerating package names (not an actual install)
  • A pinned reference in documentation/ticket text captured by a shell (no real fetch)
  • Security tooling querying npm for the version to check exposure
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command actually installed (vs. referenced) the version and identify the host/build agent and whether the library was subsequently loaded (node process launch). 2) Contain: remove the malicious versions, pin to last-safe (3.3.0/1.1.0/0.7.0/6.11.1), purge node_modules and caches, and rotate all developer/CI secrets since Miasma harvests npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host and CI runner with these versions, then correlate with the C2 (85.137.53.71), sync.js drop, and node -e launcher detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
