FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262: admin takeover via leaked logkey reuse to /AdminPlugins AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a source IP that sent the parenthesis-bypass SQLi against /api/3 with a subsequent HTTP 200 to admin routes (/AdminPlugins, /AdminHome). In the PoC the SQLi leaked the admin logkey cookie, which was replayed to reach the admin plugin-management UI — this is the account-takeover step. Rationale: Encodes the article's end-to-end takeover: the leaked logkey cookie was injected into a fresh jar and 'GET /AdminPlugins returned 200 with the admin plugin management UI.' Correlating a 200 to /AdminPlugins or /AdminHome from the same SrcIp that submitted the filter[] parenthesis SQLi is high-fidelity because normal API clients never touch the admin UI. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/
ATT&CKT1078 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine administrator who both uses the API and manages plugins from the same egress IP (small single-tenant deployments)
  • Shared corporate NAT/proxy where API traffic and admin browsing exit the same public IP
  • Vulnerability scanner that crawls both /api/3 and /Admin* routes in one authorised assessment
  • Load balancer health checks or synthetic monitors hitting admin endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SqliFirst timestamp precedes the /AdminPlugins 200, and that the SrcIp's SQLi query carried a real UNION/nick= payload. Compare the SrcIp against the admin's known office/VPN ranges. 2) Contain: invalidate all active FacturaScripts sessions (rotate logkey/secret), force admin credential reset, disable/rotate every ApiKey, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: enumerate other /Admin* routes hit by the SrcIp (plugin installs, user creation), review FacturaScripts audit/plugin directories for newly added plugins or webshells, and check for outbound connections from the FacturaScripts host.

FacturaScripts /api/3/clientes response-size anomaly (SQLi data dump) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags /api/3/clientes responses whose body is far larger than the endpoint's baseline while the request carries a filter[] parameter — the signature of a UNION SELECT dumping the users table (password hash + logkey) through the clientes serialiser. Distinct pivot from the request-signature UC: it catches a successful exfil even if the payload encoding evaded the request-side rule. Rationale: The article states the injected UNION mirrors the clientes table's 32 columns so the leaked admin hash/logkey are returned inside the JSON 'cifnif' key — a successful dump inflates the response body well above a normal clientes read. Pairing the size anomaly with the presence of a filter[] parameter keeps it article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/
ATT&CKT1190 T1005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bulk exports / large limit= page reads of the clientes list
  • Reporting or ETL integrations that pull the full customer table
  • First run after a data import when clientes row count spikes
  • A tenant with genuinely large customer records (long notes/addresses) skewing the P95
Suppression filter
| where not(DecodedUrl contains "limit=" and not(DecodedUrl contains "(")) // keep injection-shaped filters, drop plain large paged reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request's filter[] value for parenthesis + UNION/SELECT tokens and the SrcIp; a legitimate bulk read will use limit=/offset= not a parenthesised filter key. 2) Contain: if the filter carries injection syntax, treat as confirmed dump — rotate admin credentials, all ApiKeys and the app secret, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: review the same SrcIp for /api/3 requests against other resources (proveedores, users, attachedfiles) and for subsequent admin-UI access via leaked logkey.
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
    | where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
    | summarize P95 = percentile(HttpResponseBodyBytes, 95);
let P95Bytes = toscalar(Baseline | project P95);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
| where DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > (P95Bytes * 3)    // 3x the 95th-percentile normal clientes response body
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpResponseBodyBytes, P95Bytes, HttpStatusCode
| order by HttpResponseBodyBytes desc

FacturaScripts filter[] SQLi obfuscation: multiple distinct encodings from one source AIExploitation Medium
Detects a single source submitting several distinct encodings of a filter[] SQL-injection payload (mixed %28/%29, %20, /**/, case variation) to the /api/3 API within a short window — WAF-evasion / payload-tuning behaviour against the CVE-2026-45262 parenthesis bypass. Aggregation pivot on source, complementary to the single-request signature rule. Rationale: The article's PoC mixes literal syntax with %20/%28/%5B encoding and comment tokens (-- ); an attacker tuning the parenthesis bypass against a WAF will emit multiple distinct encodings of the same logical filter payload. Keying dcount on the raw (encoded) filter token surfaces that variation while the decoded-token filter keeps it scoped to SQLi attempts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5qmh-x653-g8qj
ATT&CKT1027 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised DAST/sqlmap runs which by design mutate payload encodings rapidly
  • A buggy client retrying the same filter with slightly different URL-encoding libraries
  • Fuzzing during QA of a new API integration
  • Browser vs. mobile-app clients double-encoding the same legitimate filter differently
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the make_set of FilterPayloads for the SrcIp — confirm they are encoding variants of a UNION/SELECT/parenthesis payload rather than distinct legitimate filters. 2) Contain: block the SrcIp at the WAF and add a virtual-patch rule rejecting /api/3 filter[] keys containing '(' + ')' with SQL verbs; confirm FacturaScripts is patched. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the variants returned HTTP 200 with an inflated body (successful bypass) and pivot the SrcIp to the admin-takeover and response-size detections.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/" and DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "(", "sleep(", "information_schema")
| extend FilterPayload = extract(@"filter[^&]*", 0, tolower(Url))    // raw (still-encoded) filter token so different encodings stay distinct
| summarize DistinctPayloads = dcount(FilterPayload), Payloads = make_set(FilterPayload, 10), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctPayloads > 3        // >3 distinct filter[] encodings in 5 min = WAF-evasion / payload tuning
| order by DistinctPayloads desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/3/*" (Web.uri_query="*filter*") (Web.uri_query="*union*" OR Web.uri_query="*UNION*" OR Web.uri_query="*select*" OR Web.uri_query="*SELECT*" OR Web.uri_query="*%28*" OR Web.uri_query="*(*") by Web.src, Web.uri_query, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats dc(uri_query) as distinct_payloads count as requests values(uri_query) as payloads by Web.src, _time | where distinct_payloads > 3

LabubaRAT nvidia-sysruntime.exe launch with runtime C2 config in command line AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the LabubaRAT loader binary 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' that impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit and takes its C2 server (pipicka.xyz) and polling interval as launch arguments — or as a single Base64-encoded argument. Article-specific because the same compiled binary is re-tasked per campaign purely via command line. Rationale: Pivots on the exact named loader 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' plus the hard IOC pipicka.xyz appearing in the launch arguments (article states C2 + polling interval are passed at runtime, optionally Base64-encoded). Cross-checked against SC Media and the KSEC intel forum. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Red-team engagement replaying LabubaRAT TTPs
  • EDR sample-submission automation renaming test binaries to 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe'

| where not(FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")

1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any Base64 argument to recover the C2 host + polling interval; confirm the binary is NOT signed by NVIDIA and not under \Program Files\NVIDIA. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host and kill/quarantine nvidia-sysruntime.exe and its SQLite config DB. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/filename org-wide, look for pipicka.xyz DNS/HTTPS beacons, Run-key persistence, and the AV-enumeration behavior on the same host.

LabubaRAT C2 beacon to pipicka.xyz (HTTPS / DNS tunneling) from NVIDIA-impersonating host AICommand & Control High
Hunts network and DNS traffic to the LabubaRAT C2 domain pipicka.xyz, including data-carrying subdomains characteristic of the implant's DNS-tunneling communication path. Article-specific because pipicka.xyz is the confirmed default C2 and DNS tunneling is one of its three named channels (HTTPS, WebView2, DNS). Rationale: pipicka.xyz is the confirmed hard C2 IOC; the subdomain-length logic surfaces the DNS-tunneling channel the article explicitly names. Corroborated by SC Media. Sentinel query rewritten to use DnsEvents.Name/ClientIP (not the invalid IPAddresses column) and ImDnsActivity.DnsQuery. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/DNS-sinkhole platforms actively resolving pipicka.xyz for enrichment
  • Security appliances pre-resolving IOC domains from a feed
  • Analyst manually querying the domain during investigation from a corporate workstation
  • Passive-DNS / URL-detonation sandbox traffic
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","ti-","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ContextProcess/InitiatingProcess behind the query — confirm it is nvidia-sysruntime.exe or another non-NVIDIA binary; inspect subdomain entropy/length for tunneled data. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block pipicka.xyz at the resolver and firewall, isolate the querying host. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts resolving *.pipicka.xyz in 30d, correlate with nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and Run-key persistence; capture beaconing interval to recover the polling-interval config.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "pipicka.xyz" or RemoteUrl contains ".pipicka.xyz"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".pipicka.xyz")[0])
| extend TunnelingSuspected = iff(strlen(Subdomain) > 30, "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, TunnelingSuspected
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=DvcHostname, Query=DnsQuery, Src2="", Source=EventProduct),
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=ClientIP, Host=Computer, Query=Name, Src2=QueryType, Source="MicrosoftDNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationDnsDomain has "pipicka.xyz" or RequestURL has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Query=coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), Src2=DestinationIP, Source=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-branded process spawns shell / LOLBin (LabubaRAT operator tasking) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any process whose image name starts with 'nvidia' spawning cmd/powershell/script hosts/LOLBins — legitimate NVIDIA software does not launch interactive shells. Captures LabubaRAT's command-execution, PowerShell-execution and JavaScript-execution operator capabilities running under its NVIDIA masquerade. Rationale: Article states LabubaRAT masquerades as NVIDIA software and supports command/PowerShell/JavaScript execution; genuine NVIDIA binaries never parent interactive shells, making the nvidia-parent → shell-child pair high-signal for the malware's operator tasking. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GeForce Experience / NVIDIA installer legitimately shelling out to run driver-cleanup scripts
  • NVIDIA telemetry or crash-reporter invoking rundll32 during driver install
  • IT deployment tooling wrapping a renamed nvidia*.exe launcher
  • Third-party 'nvidia'-prefixed OEM utility spawning cmd for a config task
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the parent nvidia*.exe signer and path — genuine NVIDIA lives under \Program Files\NVIDIA and is Authenticode-signed by NVIDIA; inspect the child command line for discovery/download activity. 2) Contain: if parent is unsigned/misplaced, isolate host and quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: check the same host for pipicka.xyz beacons, Run-key persistence, and AV/browser enumeration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName contains "\\nvidia" and ParentProcessName endswith ".exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-named executable without valid NVIDIA code signature AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of binaries whose filename starts with 'nvidia' but whose embedded company/signer is not NVIDIA — the core file-level masquerade LabubaRAT relies on (impersonating NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit). Flags nvidia-sysruntime.exe and any re-branded variant that fails to chain to NVIDIA's trusted publisher. Rationale: Directly operationalizes the article's 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise: Defender's ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName lets us flag nvidia-named binaries whose signer isn't NVIDIA. Sentinel left blank because SecurityEvent 4688 carries no signer/company field to express the mismatch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OEM/laptop-vendor NVIDIA helper utilities signed under the OEM's name rather than NVIDIA
  • Portable NVIDIA tools run from a user Downloads folder before install
  • Older NVIDIA components with stripped/blank version metadata
  • Internal software-packaging wrappers that re-sign an nvidia launcher with a corporate cert
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Dell","HP","Lenovo","ASUS","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: compute the SHA256 and check reputation; confirm the file is the LabubaRAT loader vs a legitimately OEM-signed helper. 2) Contain: quarantine the binary and isolate the host if the hash is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: sweep org-wide for the same hash/filename, then correlate with pipicka.xyz C2 and Run-key persistence on affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LabubaRAT user-level autostart persistence (Run key / scheduled task referencing NVIDIA loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Run/RunOnce registry writes or scheduled-task creation that reference the LabubaRAT loader (nvidia-sysruntime) or its C2 (pipicka.xyz), or that are written by an nvidia-named process — the 'user level autostart' persistence the article says LabubaRAT maintains. Rationale: Article explicitly notes LabubaRAT maintains 'user level autostart'; keying Run-key value data on the named loader and pipicka.xyz IOC keeps this tight while the nvidia-writer clause catches renamed variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine NVIDIA GeForce Experience / driver auto-update writing an nvidia Run entry from \Program Files\NVIDIA
  • Software-deployment tooling staging an nvidia launcher in Run for post-reboot install
  • Backup/imaging solution restoring a legacy Run value
  • Analyst re-adding a known-good nvidia autostart during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Run value data and confirm the referenced binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader (not \Program Files\NVIDIA). 2) Contain: delete the autostart value/task, quarantine the referenced binary, isolate host. 3) Hunt: check for the same value across the fleet and correlate with pipicka.xyz beaconing and loader execution.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent

| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or ActingProcessName contains "\\nvidia"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized NVIDIA installer download from non-NVIDIA source AIDelivery Medium
Hunts creation/download of an nvidia-named executable whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is NOT an NVIDIA domain, or that is written to disk by a browser/mail client — the delivery vector for the fake NVIDIA container-runtime installer that drops LabubaRAT. Rationale: The 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise implies a fake installer; keying an nvidia-named exe on a non-NVIDIA origin URL (mark-of-the-web) or a browser/mail-client writer surfaces the delivery without alerting on legitimate NVIDIA downloads. Sigma/Datadog omitted because origin-URL is not a standard field for those log shapes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users downloading NVIDIA drivers from a legitimate mirror/CDN not on the allowlist (e.g. an OEM or Steam-hosted redistributable)
  • Internal software portal re-hosting NVIDIA installers on a corporate URL
  • Driver-management tools (Snappy/Chocolatey) fetching nvidia packages
  • Archived nvidia installer copied from a file share and re-tagged with a referrer URL
Suppression filter
| where not(FileOriginUrl has_any ("chocolatey.org","steamstatic.com") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FileOriginUrl + referrer and SHA256; confirm the source domain is attacker-controlled and the file is unsigned/non-NVIDIA. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the source domain at the proxy, and check whether it was executed. 3) Hunt: search EmailUrlInfo/EmailAttachmentInfo for the same lure, and sweep the fleet for the hash plus subsequent nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and pipicka.xyz traffic.

| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)
| where not(FileOriginUrl has "nvidia.com" or FileOriginUrl has "nvidia.cn" or FileOriginUrl has "download.nvidia.com" or FileOriginUrl has "nvidia.co")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"

NVIDIA-branded process outbound to non-NVIDIA public infrastructure (LabubaRAT C2 / SOCKS5 proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioral C2 hunt: any nvidia-named process making public network connections to destinations that are NOT NVIDIA infrastructure. Catches LabubaRAT's HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxy traffic even when the operator swaps out pipicka.xyz for fresh infrastructure (the article stresses the binary is re-tasked per campaign). Rationale: Behavioral complement to the pipicka.xyz IOC hunt: legitimate NVIDIA software talks only to NVIDIA/CDN infrastructure, so an nvidia-named process reaching arbitrary public IPs/domains captures LabubaRAT's re-taskable HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxying. Sentinel left blank — this tenant's Sentinel network tables (ImNetworkSession/CommonSecurityLog) don't carry the initiating process image needed to bind the connection to nvidia*.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NVIDIA software contacting a licensing/telemetry endpoint on a non-nvidia.com CDN (Akamai/Cloudflare edge)
  • GeForce Experience pulling game-ready driver assets from a third-party CDN
  • OEM nvidia utility phoning home to the OEM's domain
  • Crash-reporter uploading to a non-NVIDIA error-aggregation service
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the remote IP/domain and check reputation/passive-DNS; confirm the initiating binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader and assess connection periodicity for beaconing. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across the fleet, correlate with pipicka.xyz DNS, Run-key persistence, and loader execution; review for SOCKS5 listener/relay behavior.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "nvidia.com" or RemoteUrl has "nvidia.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith "nvidia.co")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "nvidia.com" or RemoteUrl has "nvidia.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith "nvidia.co")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount

| tstats `summariesonly` count

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LastPass, Bitwarden users targeted with fake security alerts

BleepingComputer
2026-07-14 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

LastPass is warning users about an ongoing phishing campaign that is using fake security notices to direct them to fraudulent websites. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.001
Domainslastpassnewsletter.com lastpasscompliance.com bitwardennewsletter.com bitwardencompliance.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing from spoofed LastPass/Bitwarden 'newsletter' or 'compliance' domains · [LLM] Endpoint reaches fake-DocuSign lastpasscompliance/bitwardencompliance landing page · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Payload downloaded from fake-DocuSign compliance domain (Win/macOS installer drop)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound phishing from spoofed LastPass/Bitwarden 'newsletter' or 'compliance' domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose sender domain or embedded URL matches the campaign's spoofed infrastructure (lastpassnewsletter.com / bitwardennewsletter.com senders, lastpasscompliance.com / bitwardencompliance.com fake-DocuSign links). Article-specific because it pins the exact look-alike domains LastPass disowned rather than generic password-manager phishing. Rationale: Uses the four disowned look-alike domains and the exact 'hello@' sender addresses named by LastPass/BleepingComputer and confirmed by CyberInsider/PCWorld — a domain-exact match, not a generic brand-impersonation heuristic. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: mailflow telemetry (EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo) is Defender-for-Office-only and has no equivalent in the provided Sentinel schema or in FDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberinsider.com/lastpass-warns-users-of-active-campaign-targeting-master-passwords/ • https://www.pcworld.com/article/2944308/lastpass-and-bitwarden-password-managers-targeted-by-phishing-campaign.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/lastpass-bitwarden-spoofed-in-ongoing-phishing-campaign
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate LastPass/Bitwarden marketing mail from the real vendor domains (lastpass.com / bitwarden.com) — will NOT match because the query pins the look-alike domains only, so effectively no benign match unless someone registers the same string for legit use.
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation vendor replaying this exact campaign template (KnowBe4/Proofpoint sim).
  • An internal researcher forwarding a captured sample to a reporting mailbox (mail becomes Intra-org / different NetworkMessageId).
  • Threat-intel feed digest email that quotes the domains in body text (matched only if the domain appears as a live URL, not plain text).
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matched NetworkMessageId, confirm DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation — was it Delivered to Inbox or already Junked/Quarantined? Identify all recipients and whether any URL click exists in UrlClickEvents. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer/ZAP, block the sender + compliance domains at the mail gateway and add lastpasscompliance.com/bitwardencompliance.com to network URL block lists. 3) Hunt: for any recipient who clicked, pivot to UC-2/UC-3 (network egress to the compliance domains and installer drop); reset the vault master password from a trusted device for anyone who reached the fake DocuSign page.
let CampaignSenderDomains = dynamic(["lastpassnewsletter.com","bitwardennewsletter.com"]);
let CampaignUrlDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
let UrlHits = EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where UrlDomain in~ (CampaignUrlDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (CampaignSenderDomains)
   or SenderMailFromDomain in~ (CampaignSenderDomains)
   or SenderFromAddress in~ ("hello@lastpassnewsletter.com","hello@bitwardennewsletter.com")
   or NetworkMessageId in ((UrlHits | project NetworkMessageId))
| join kind=leftouter UrlHits on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let CampaignSenderDomains = dynamic(["lastpassnewsletter.com","bitwardennewsletter.com"]);
let CampaignUrlDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
let UrlHits = EmailUrlInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where UrlDomain in~ (CampaignUrlDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain;
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (CampaignSenderDomains)
   or SenderMailFromDomain in~ (CampaignSenderDomains)
   or SenderFromAddress in~ ("hello@lastpassnewsletter.com","hello@bitwardennewsletter.com")
   or NetworkMessageId in ((UrlHits | project NetworkMessageId))
| join kind=leftouter UrlHits on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Endpoint reaches fake-DocuSign lastpasscompliance/bitwardencompliance landing page AIDelivery High
Detects a host resolving or connecting to the campaign's fake-DocuSign landing domains (lastpasscompliance.com / bitwardencompliance.com) — the click-through step where the victim is prompted to download the Win/macOS payload. Article-specific because it keys on the exact Microsoft/Cloudflare-flagged domains, not generic 'browser hits a URL'. Rationale: Pins the two fake-DocuSign landing domains that Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Cloudflare independently flagged as malicious (per BleepingComputer/SC Media), so any resolution or connection is high-fidelity — legitimate LastPass/Bitwarden traffic uses lastpass.com/bitwarden.com. CloudWatch left empty (no AWS telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/lastpass-bitwarden-spoofed-in-ongoing-phishing-campaign • https://cyberinsider.com/lastpass-warns-users-of-active-campaign-targeting-master-passwords/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel researcher manually browsing the domain in a sandbox/VM to triage the campaign.
  • Security web-proxy or URL-detonation service (e.g. Defender Safe Links sandbox) resolving the domain during automated scanning.
  • A DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it redirects the victim — appears as a hit but is actually the block working.
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection tooling that periodically resolves newly-registered look-alike domains.
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host + user that reached the domain and the initiating process (browser vs. non-browser). Check whether the connection succeeded or was blocked/sinkholed, and whether it came right after a UC-1 email click. 2) Contain: block both domains + resolved IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, and isolate the host if a file download followed (pivot to UC-3). 3) Hunt: search the same host for a subsequently written installer (UC-3), and reset the vault master password from a trusted device for the user, since the landing page harvests credentials before the download prompt.
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let ClickHits = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any (CampaignDomains)
    | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress;
union
  (NetHits | extend Source = "DeviceNetwork"),
  (ClickHits | extend Source = "UrlClick", DeviceName = "", AccountName = AccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName = "", RemoteUrl = Url, RemoteIP = tostring(IPAddress))
| project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Fake-DocuSign LastPass/Bitwarden Compliance Domains
id: 8f3a1c62-4b7e-4d19-9a2c-2f6e1d0b7c44
description: Detects DNS resolution of the lastpasscompliance.com / bitwardencompliance.com domains used in the July 2026 fake-DocuSign phishing campaign impersonating LastPass and Bitwarden.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lastpass-bitwarden-users-targeted-with-fake-security-alerts/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - 'lastpasscompliance.com'
      - 'bitwardencompliance.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(lastpasscompliance.com OR bitwardencompliance.com OR *.lastpasscompliance.com OR *.bitwardencompliance.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)(lastpasscompliance|bitwardencompliance)\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
Payload downloaded from fake-DocuSign compliance domain (Win/macOS installer drop) AIInstallation High
Detects a file written to disk whose download origin URL is the campaign's fake-DocuSign domains (lastpasscompliance.com / bitwardencompliance.com), catching the cross-platform 'installer' the site prompts victims to save. Article-specific via FileOriginUrl matching the exact malicious domains rather than a generic 'browser dropped an exe'. Rationale: Anchors on FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl equal to the two malicious fake-DocuSign domains, so it fires only on files actually pulled from campaign infrastructure — no filename/hash was published, making mark-of-the-web download origin the only reliable article-grounded pivot. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: download-origin URL provenance (FileOriginUrl) is a Defender-only field with no equivalent in ImFileEvent, Sysmon EID 11, or FileWritten. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lastpass-bitwarden-users-targeted-with-fake-security-alerts/ • https://www.pcworld.com/article/2944308/lastpass-and-bitwarden-password-managers-targeted-by-phishing-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst detonating the sample in a managed VM to capture the payload for analysis.
  • EDR/sandbox automated file collection re-writing the same download to a quarantine path (retains original FileOriginUrl).
  • No benign business download realistically originates from these look-alike domains, so true FPs are limited to security-team investigation activity.
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture FileName, FolderPath, SHA256 and the initiating browser/process; determine if the file was executed (pivot SHA256 into DeviceProcessEvents) and whether it is the Windows or macOS variant. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine/block the SHA256 tenant-wide, and revoke the user's password-manager session + force master-password reset from a trusted device. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same SHA256 and for any file with FileOriginUrl on the campaign domains; submit the hash to VT/ThreatFox and check for follow-on C2 or persistence on the affected host.
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileOriginUrl has_any (CampaignDomains) or FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["lastpasscompliance.com","bitwardencompliance.com"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileOriginUrl has_any (CampaignDomains) or FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] RedSun (CVE-2026-41091) overwrite of System32\TieringEngineService.exe for SYSTEM execution · Article-specific behavioural hunt — You Don't Have to Run an Exploit to Know If You're Vulnerable
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] UnDefend tampering with Windows Defender signature files (mpavbase.vdm / mpavbase.lkg) · [LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse 'Evilsvc' SYSTEM service creation (BlueHammer / BAS emulation) · Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hive access via Defender-created Volume Shadow Copy · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hive access via Defender-created Volume Shadow Copy AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the BlueHammer credential-theft primitive: a non-SYSTEM process reading the SAM, SYSTEM, or SECURITY registry hives out of a Volume Shadow Copy snapshot that Defender's remediation workflow created (triggered by an EICAR bait file). Distinct from LSASS dumping — this is offline hive extraction from a shadow-copy path. Rationale: Uses the exact BlueHammer primitive from the article — reading SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives out of the Defender-generated Volume Shadow Copy (path token 'HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy'). Corroborated by CVEReports and PT Security which confirm VSS is chained to snapshot the SAM hive. Sentinel path requires SACL object-access auditing on the hive files; Sysmon has no read-event so Datadog/Sigma omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-33825 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup software (Veeam, Windows Server Backup/wbengine) reading hives from shadow copies as SYSTEM
  • Forensic collection tooling (KAPE, FTK Imager, Velociraptor) staging registry hives from VSS
  • DC replication / SYSVOL operations touching SYSTEM hive under a snapshot
  • Sysadmin restoring registry from a shadow copy during troubleshooting
  • EDR/DLP agents scanning shadow-copy contents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("wbengine.exe","veeamagent.exe","vssvc.exe","kape.exe","ftkimager.exe","velociraptor.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating account is an unprivileged user (not machine/SYSTEM/backup service) and check for a preceding Defender EICAR detection or MpSigStub-created shadow copy on the same host in the prior minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, reset all local accounts (hashes in SAM are now exposed) and any cached domain creds, and force-remove the shadow copy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet, look for follow-on 'Evilsvc' service creation and TieringEngineService.exe writes (RedSun) indicating the full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("SAM","SYSTEM","SECURITY")
| where FolderPath has "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName has "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy"
| where ObjectName has_any ("\\SAM","\\SYSTEM","\\SECURITY")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessName, ObjectName, AccessMask, HandleId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy/i
| TargetFileName=/(SAM|SYSTEM|SECURITY)$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(MsMpEng|MpSigStub|VeeamAgent|wbengine)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("SAM","SYSTEM","SECURITY")) AND Filesystem.file_path="*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*" by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("SAM","SYSTEM","SECURITY")) AND Filesystem.file_path="*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*" by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
RedSun (CVE-2026-41091) overwrite of System32\TieringEngineService.exe for SYSTEM execution AIExploitation High
Hunts the RedSun privileged-write primitive: a non-servicing process modifying or replacing C:\Windows\System32\TieringEngineService.exe with an attacker binary, which is then launched as SYSTEM via the Storage Tiers Management COM object. The target binary is only ever changed by Windows servicing, making any other writer high-signal. Rationale: Keys on the exact RedSun target from the article — an attacker binary overwriting C:\Windows\System32\TieringEngineService.exe then executed via the Storage Tiers Management COM object as SYSTEM. This service binary is only legitimately modified by Windows servicing (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker), so a non-servicing writer is near-zero FP. RedSun mapped to CVE-2026-41091 via Cyderes/search corroboration (article named only BlueHammer's CVE). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/redsun-zero-day • https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy • https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1574.010
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/feature update servicing TieringEngineService.exe via TiWorker/TrustedInstaller
  • In-place OS upgrade replacing System32 binaries
  • SCCM/WSUS patch deployment touching the service binary
  • Third-party disk-tiering software installer (rare) staging the binary
  • Backup restore rewriting System32 files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","poqexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel =~ "System")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the new SHA256 of TieringEngineService.exe and verify Microsoft signature; check whether the initiating process was a servicing binary — if not, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill/quarantine the replaced binary, restore the legitimate signed TieringEngineService.exe, and revoke SYSTEM-derived tokens/sessions. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the BlueHammer SAM-via-VSS access and 'Evilsvc' service creation to scope the full Nightmare-Eclipse chain; sweep the fleet for the attacker binary hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "TieringEngineService.exe"
| where FolderPath has "System32"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","poqexec.exe","msiexec.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, FolderPath, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "TieringEngineService.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has "System32"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("TrustedInstaller","TiWorker","poqexec","msiexec","MoUsoCoreWorker"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RedSun System32 TieringEngineService.exe Overwrite (CVE-2026-41091)
id: 8f2c1a44-9d3e-4b21-8a77-1c9e5f0a2b31
description: Detects modification or replacement of the Storage Tiers Management service binary TieringEngineService.exe by a non-servicing process, the RedSun (Nightmare-Eclipse) SYSTEM-execution primitive.
references:
  - https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/redsun-zero-day
  - https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1543.003
  - attack.t1574.010
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\System32\TieringEngineService.exe'
  filter_servicing:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'
      - '\TiWorker.exe'
      - '\poqexec.exe'
      - '\msiexec.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_servicing
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\System32\\TieringEngineService.exe OR *\\System32\\tieringengineservice.exe) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\poqexec.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/TieringEngineService\.exe$/i
| regex("System32", field=TargetFileName)
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|poqexec|msiexec|MoUsoCoreWorker)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="TieringEngineService.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*System32*" AND Filesystem.action IN ("modified","created","deleted","renamed") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="TieringEngineService.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*System32*" AND Filesystem.action IN ("modified","created","deleted","renamed") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
UnDefend tampering with Windows Defender signature files (mpavbase.vdm / mpavbase.lkg) AIInstallation High
Hunts the UnDefend defense-evasion tool: a non-Defender process locking, overwriting, or deleting Defender's signature base files mpavbase.vdm and mpavbase.lkg to freeze definition updates and block the signature base from reloading, while the console still reports healthy. Only Defender's own binaries should touch these files. Rationale: Directly targets the UnDefend artifacts named in the article — the Defender signature files mpavbase.vdm and mpavbase.lkg being locked/blocked from reload. Excluding Defender's own signature-update binaries (MsMpEng/MpSigStub/MpCmdRun) leaves only tampering. Corroborated by Lyrie and Huntress as part of the observed Nightmare-Eclipse chain. Cross-checked against: • https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy • https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender platform/engine upgrade rewriting the signature base outside the usual MpSigStub context
  • Manual signature rollback via MpCmdRun -RemoveDefinitions
  • Endpoint backup/imaging tool snapshotting the Definition Updates folder
  • AV migration removing Defender definitions during third-party AV install
  • Disk-cleanup/optimizer touching ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Windows Defender" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","NisSrv.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and confirm it is not a Defender component; check Defender health/last-signature-update timestamp for a stall despite 'healthy' status (the UnDefend tell). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the tampering process, force 'Update-MpSignature' / MpCmdRun -SignatureUpdate and restart WinDefend to restore live protection. 3) Hunt: correlate with BlueHammer VSS hive access and RedSun TieringEngineService.exe writes on the same host and timeframe; sweep for the tampering binary hash fleet-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("mpavbase.vdm","mpavbase.lkg")
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","NisSrv.exe","MsMpEngCP.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Windows Defender"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("mpavbase.vdm","mpavbase.lkg")
| where EventType in~ ("FileModified","FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("MsMpEng","MpSigStub","MpCmdRun","MpDefenderCoreService","NisSrv"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UnDefend Tampering with Defender Signature Base (Nightmare-Eclipse)
id: 3b6d90e2-71af-4c58-b2d4-9a0c7e1f4d82
description: Detects a non-Defender process modifying, deleting or renaming the Windows Defender signature base files mpavbase.vdm / mpavbase.lkg, the UnDefend defense-evasion technique that freezes definition reloads while reporting healthy.
references:
  - https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\mpavbase.vdm'
      - '\mpavbase.lkg'
  filter_defender:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\MpSigStub.exe'
      - '\MpCmdRun.exe'
      - '\MpDefenderCoreService.exe'
      - '\NisSrv.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_defender
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*mpavbase.vdm* OR *mpavbase.lkg* OR *MPAVBASE.VDM* OR *MPAVBASE.LKG*) -@Image:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\MpSigStub.exe OR *\\MpCmdRun.exe OR *\\NisSrv.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/mpavbase\.(vdm|lkg)$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(MsMpEng|MpSigStub|MpCmdRun|NisSrv|MpDefenderCoreService)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("mpavbase.vdm","mpavbase.lkg") AND Filesystem.action IN ("modified","deleted","renamed") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("mpavbase.vdm","mpavbase.lkg") AND Filesystem.action IN ("modified","deleted","renamed") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.action, Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Nightmare-Eclipse 'Evilsvc' SYSTEM service creation (BlueHammer / BAS emulation) AIInstallation High
Alerts on creation of a Windows service named 'Evilsvc' — the final SYSTEM-execution step of the BlueHammer chain (CreateService) and the Picus BAS emulation artifact. No legitimate software installs a service by this name, making the literal name a near-zero-FP tripwire for the emulated or real chain. Rationale: The literal service name 'Evilsvc' is named in the article as both BlueHammer's CreateService execution step and the Picus emulation action; no legitimate product uses it, so exact-name matching is a high-fidelity, low-FP alert. Registry \Services\Evilsvc and 7045 ServiceInstalled are the canonical creation signals. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/you-dont-have-to-run-an-exploit-to-know-if-youre-vulnerable/ • https://lyrie.ai/research/research/cve-2026-33825-bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-lpe-trilogy
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized Picus / BAS validation run in production (this IS the emulation artifact)
  • Internal red-team or purple-team exercise reproducing the chain
  • Security researcher testing the public PoC in a lab that reports to prod telemetry
  • A benign in-house tool coincidentally named Evilsvc (near-zero)
  • Atomic Red Team style adversary-emulation testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether an authorized BAS/red-team window is active — if so, mark benign; otherwise check the service ImagePath and the initiating account/integrity level (SYSTEM via BlueHammer). 2) Contain: isolate host, stop and delete the Evilsvc service, quarantine its ImagePath binary, and reset local + any exposed domain credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for BlueHammer VSS SAM access, RedSun TieringEngineService.exe overwrite, and UnDefend signature-file tampering to establish the full Nightmare-Eclipse chain; sweep the fleet for the service ImagePath hash.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where AdditionalFields has "Evilsvc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName =~ "Evilsvc"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nightmare-Eclipse Evilsvc Service Creation
id: c1e7a2f0-4b8d-4e39-9f61-2d3a6b8c0e57

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33825")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33825")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental
description: |

            - '\remcom.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Service Persistence via sc.exe with User-Writable Path
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0e
status: experimental
description: |
    sc.exe create with the binary path under \Users\, \AppData\,
    \ProgramData\, or \Temp\ — service-install persistence outside
    legitimate program directories.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\AppData\'
            - '\ProgramData\'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry

            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
