Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c

Unauthenticated GET /api/auth on RabbitMQ management port leaking OAuth client secret (CVE-2026-57219) AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to the obsolete RabbitMQ management HTTP endpoint GET /api/auth on port 15672, which returns the broker's OAuth client secret to any unauthenticated caller. Focuses on external/untrusted source IPs hitting the exact path, since the endpoint's authz check was hard-coded to always allow. Rationale: Pivots on the exact obsolete path '/api/auth' plus the RabbitMQ management port 15672 named in the disclosure; because every other sensitive management endpoint requires auth, GET /api/auth returning 200 is a near-unique high-fidelity signal.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RabbitMQ management UI automation/health checks polling /api/ endpoints from internal monitoring hosts
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing /api/auth during authorized scans
  • Internal admin browsing the management UI whose session hits /api/auth
  • Load balancer health probes configured against the management API
Suppression filter
| where not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting SrcIpAddr is external/untrusted and the response status was 200 (secret returned); check whether the instance uses management.oauth_client_secret. 2) Contain: block port 15672 from untrusted networks, patch to 4.3.0/4.2.6/4.1.11/4.0.20/3.13.15, and immediately rotate the OAuth client secret. 3) Hunt: search AAD/OAuth token issuance and RabbitMQ admin API calls from the leaked secret for follow-on admin-token exchange and queue/user/config changes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where Url has "/api/auth"
| where DstPortNumber == 15672 or Url has ":15672"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-tenant RabbitMQ queue/exchange enumeration via management API (CVE-2026-57221) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source enumerating many queue and exchange names through the RabbitMQ management API (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) on port 15672, abusing the missing authorization that lets any connected vhost user read all queue/exchange names, message counts and consumer counts regardless of permissions. Rationale: Uses the specific management API resource paths (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) and port 15672 tied to the missing-authz flaw; a source pulling >20 distinct queue/exchange paths in a short window is the enumeration behaviour the CVE enables, whereas normal management UI use touches few endpoints.
ATT&CKT1087 T1580
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RabbitMQ management UI overview page auto-refreshing and paging through the full queue/exchange list for a legitimate admin
  • Monitoring exporters (rabbitmq_exporter / Prometheus) scraping /api/queues and /api/exchanges on a schedule
  • Capacity/inventory tooling walking all vhosts for reporting
  • CI pipelines validating broker topology across many queues
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("monitoring-host-ip-not-known") and not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) and DstHostname has "exporter")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the authenticated user behind SrcIpAddr and compare their assigned vhost permissions to the breadth of queues/exchanges enumerated; legit monitoring accounts are expected, ad-hoc user accounts are not. 2) Contain: restrict port 15672 to trusted management networks, separate tenants by vhost, and patch to the fixed release lines. 3) Hunt: review whether the same principal then consumed messages or authenticated to queues outside its tenant, and correlate with any /api/auth secret-leak hits.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where DstPortNumber == 15672 or Url has ":15672"
| where Url has_any ("/api/queues", "/api/exchanges")
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(Url), SampledPaths = make_set(Url, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctPaths > 20   // bulk queue/exchange name enumeration in one window
| order by DistinctPaths desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.dest_port=15672 (Web.uri_path="/api/queues*" OR Web.uri_path="/api/exchanges*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths sum(count) as totalRequests values(uri_path) as sampledPaths by src, dest
| where distinctPaths > 20
| sort - distinctPaths
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.dest_port=15672 (Web.uri_path="/api/queues*" OR Web.uri_path="/api/exchanges*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths sum(count) as totalRequests values(uri_path) as sampledPaths by src, dest
| where distinctPaths > 20
| sort - distinctPaths

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Successful Entra ID sign-in via OAuth 2.0 device code flow (Jalisco/EvilTokens device-code phishing) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Multiple rogue Entra device registrations named 'Microsoft'/'Windows' on one account
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Successful Entra ID sign-in via OAuth 2.0 device code flow (Jalisco/EvilTokens device-code phishing) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful interactive Microsoft Entra sign-ins that used the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flow, the core primitive the Jalisco kit abuses to authorize an attacker-controlled device without ever needing the victim's password or triggering a standard MFA prompt. ReliaQuest notes device-code auth should be blocked entirely via Conditional Access, so any success is worth review. Rationale: Article states Jalisco 'generates fresh Microsoft OAuth device codes automatically' and abuses the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flow; the deviceCode auth protocol on a successful sign-in is the single highest-fidelity in-telemetry marker of this class of kit. AuthenticationProcessingDetails is used because it is the device-code indicator present in the provided Defender/Sentinel schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/device-code-phishing-hits-340-microsoft.html • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/device-code-phishing-campaign • https://cyberwarrior76.substack.com/p/mfa-is-not-enough-the-device-code
ATT&CKT1528 T1566
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Azure CLI / Az PowerShell 'az login --use-device-code' by engineers on headless hosts
  • IoT / smart-TV / conference-room device enrollment that legitimately uses device code flow
  • Developers authenticating VS Code or GitHub Actions runners against Microsoft Graph via device code
  • Admin onboarding of a shared kiosk device where password entry on the device is impractical
Suppression filter
| where not(AppDisplayName in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Visual Studio Code") and ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user genuinely initiated a device-code login (call/Teams them out-of-band); check IPAddress/Country/UserAgent against their normal pattern and whether the resource app is one they'd realistically use device code for. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions' in Entra), force password reset, and require re-MFA; disable the newly authorized device. 3) Hunt: pivot on the AccountUpn into UC2 (rogue device registrations named 'Microsoft'/'Windows') and UC3 (rapid SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download) for the same user within the following minutes.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0                                   // successful auth only
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" // OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, AppDisplayName,
          ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceTrustType
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0                                     // successful sign-in
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"   // OAuth 2.0 device code grant flow
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName,
          IPAddress, Location = tostring(Location), ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple rogue Entra device registrations named 'Microsoft'/'Windows' on one account AIInstallation High
Hunts a burst of device registrations against a single Entra account where the device display names contain 'Microsoft' or 'Windows' — the exact evasion ReliaQuest observed, where attackers registered up to five rogue devices per compromised account using benign-sounding names. Fires when two or more such devices are registered in a short window, matching the recommendation to lower the device-registration limit to 1-2. Rationale: Uses the two article-specific tells for the Jalisco post-compromise step: (a) device-registration operations against a compromised account and (b) benign display names containing 'Microsoft'/'Windows', with a >=2 threshold anchored to ReliaQuest's remediation advice. Threshold + temporal window makes this alerting-grade and too narrow for a single-event Sigma rule. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0036/ • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/security/8.19/microsoft-entra-id-suspicious-cloud-device-registration.html
ATT&CKT1098.005
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Autopilot / Intune bulk enrollment of newly imaged corporate laptops named per a 'Microsoft'/'Windows' naming convention
  • Helpdesk registering multiple loaner or replacement Windows devices for one user in a single session
  • A user enrolling personal Windows device + Authenticator on a phone during onboarding
  • MDM migration project re-registering a fleet under one service account
Suppression filter
| where not(Actor in~ ("intune-enroll@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com","autopilot-svc@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the registered devices for the account (Get-MgUserRegisteredDevice) and inspect DeviceTrustType, OS, and registration IP; legit enrollments come from managed/Intune contexts, rogue ones from residential/proxy IPs. 2) Contain: delete/disable the rogue device objects, revoke the user's sessions, reset credentials, and temporarily drop the tenant device-registration limit to 1. 3) Hunt: correlate the actor UPN back to UC1 (device-code sign-in that preceded this) and forward to UC3 (SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download) to scope data exposure.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where ActionType in ("Add device","Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device")
| where ObjectName has "Microsoft" or ObjectName has "Windows"   // benign-sounding rogue device names
| summarize DeviceCount = dcount(ObjectName), Devices = make_set(ObjectName, 20),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DeviceCount >= 2   // Entra default limit is 50; ReliaQuest recommends 1-2. Attackers registered up to 5.
| order by LastSeen desc

Rapid bulk SharePoint/OneDrive download by a single account (device-code extortion exfil, ~6 min) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single account downloading or syncing a large number of SharePoint/OneDrive files inside a tight time window, matching ReliaQuest's observation that after device-code account takeover attackers search SaaS repositories and exfiltrate data in as little as six minutes before extortion. Pivots on the same accounts flagged by the device-code and rogue-device UCs. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific TTP — 'exfiltration typically occurs quickly, in as little as six minutes' from SharePoint/SaaS after account takeover — as a per-user distinct-file-count threshold over a 6-minute bin. FileCount>=50 is the tunable bulk-pull line; low as a standalone signal but high-fidelity when the same UserId also appears in UC1/UC2. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/helix-data-extortion-group-uses-vishing-and-device-code-phishing/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/device-code-phishing-campaign
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1530
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive Known Folder Move / first-time client sync pulling a user's whole library after a new laptop
  • Legitimate data-migration or SharePoint tenant-to-tenant move using a service account
  • Power user / exec downloading a large project folder or archive before travel
  • eDiscovery or compliance export job running under a delegated account
  • Backup tooling (e.g. AvePoint, Veeam for M365) performing scheduled bulk reads
Suppression filter
| where not(IPs has_any (dynamic(["<corp_egress_cidr_not_used>"])) )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the download burst came from a managed device/known IP and whether the same UserId fired UC1 (device-code sign-in) or UC2 (rogue device) in the prior minutes — that correlation converts this from noisy to critical. 2) Contain: revoke sessions, reset credentials, block the source IP, and place a legal hold / suspend sharing on the affected SharePoint sites to preserve evidence. 3) Hunt: review the file names/sites accessed for PII/financial/HR content, check for outbound sync to unmanaged devices, and watch mailflow for a follow-up extortion email referencing the stolen data.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft SharePoint Online","Microsoft OneDrive for Business")
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(ObjectName), Files = make_set(ObjectName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp)
          by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 6m)
| extend WindowSeconds = datetime_diff('second', EndTime, StartTime)
| where FileCount >= 50   // bulk pull; ReliaQuest observed full exfil in ~6 minutes post-compromise
| order by EndTime desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint","OneDrive")
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed")
| where UserType != "System"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(ObjectId), Files = make_set(SourceFileName, 50), IPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10),
            StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 6m)
| extend WindowSeconds = datetime_diff('second', EndTime, StartTime)
| where FileCount >= 50   // rapid bulk access; ReliaQuest observed exfil in as little as 6 minutes
| order by EndTime desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity` (Workload=SharePoint OR Workload=OneDrive) Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed")
| bin _time span=6m
| stats dc(ObjectId) as FileCount values(SourceFileName) as Files values(ClientIP) as ClientIPs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by UserId _time
| where FileCount >= 50

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

11 Old Microsoft-Signed Linux UEFI Shims Could Let Attackers Bypass Secure Boot

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 11 old, Microsoft-signed, Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) applications that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using the modern firmware standard. "An attacker exploiting one of these vulnerable applications can execute untrusted code during system boot, enabling deployment of malicious UEFI bootkits or other malware,"

CVEsCVE-2026-8863 CVE-2026-10797
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Revoked Microsoft-signed vulnerable UEFI shim present in estate (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) · [LLM] Old shim/GRUB EFI binary written to ESP by non-package-manager process (Secure Boot bypass staging) · [LLM] MOK/SBAT enforcement disabled via mokutil (Secure Boot validation subversion)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Revoked Microsoft-signed vulnerable UEFI shim present in estate (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) AIInstallation High
Surfaces hosts carrying one of the 11 old Microsoft-signed shim bootloaders (shim 0.9 and earlier) revoked in Microsoft's June 2026 DBX update. Any device still exposing CVE-2026-8863 or CVE-2026-10797 can be used to bypass UEFI Secure Boot by bringing the still-trusted-but-unrevoked binary, so this is an exposure hunt, not a live-exploit alert. Rationale: Uses the two concrete CVE IDs assigned to the 11 revoked shims (confirmed by ESET/CERT). A pure inventory lookup — zero behavioural noise, ideal for prioritising DBX/fwupd remediation on Linux fleets that trust the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 cert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458 • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/offline lab boxes intentionally kept on old shims for reproduction
  • Appliances (Blancco WipeDrive / PC-Doctor / baramundi) that legitimately ship the affected shim as designed
  • Hosts pending a scheduled fwupd/DBX maintenance window
  • Golden images not yet re-baked after the June 2026 revocation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device trusts the Microsoft 3rd-party CA and check `mokutil --sb-state` and DBX entry count (`efi-readvar -v dbx | grep -c sha256`, expect 200+). 2) Contain: push the Microsoft June-2026 DBX/fwupd revocation update or apply the SBAT level bump so the old shim can no longer load; prioritise internet-facing and privileged-user hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that resisted DBX update, pivot to UC2/UC3 to check whether the ESP shim was actually swapped or MOK/SBAT validation was disabled.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-8863","CVE-2026-10797") by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.cve, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.signature | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-8863","CVE-2026-10797") by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.cve, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.signature | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Old shim/GRUB EFI binary written to ESP by non-package-manager process (Secure Boot bypass staging) AIInstallation Medium
Detects writes of a shim, MokManager or GRUB EFI binary into the EFI System Partition by a process that is NOT a legitimate package manager / firmware updater. This is the core of the attack: replacing the victim's up-to-date shim with an older, still-Microsoft-signed vulnerable one to reintroduce a bootkit-capable early-boot code-exec path that survives OS reinstall. Rationale: Anchors on the exact ESP artifact names (shimx64.efi / mmx64.efi / grubx64.efi) and the /boot/efi path where an attacker swaps in the old signed shim; excluding real installers/fwupd keeps the true-positive (manual/scripted replacement) sharp. ESET's core finding is that only 'a copy of an old still-trusted shim' is needed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1542.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro kernel/shim upgrade run via a wrapper the exclusion list misses (e.g. ansible/salt invoking cp directly)
  • Imaging/provisioning tools (baramundi, FOG) legitimately writing shim to ESP during deployment
  • Manual `cp`/`dd` by a sysadmin recovering an unbootable machine
  • Dual-boot setup utilities re-installing the EFI bootloader
  • Backup/restore agents rehydrating /boot/efi
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the written binary's SHA256 and compare against the distro's current signed shim; run `objdump -j .sbat -s <file>` — an absent/low-generation .sbat section on a freshly written shim is a strong signal of an old vulnerable build. Confirm the writing process/user was not a package transaction. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the vendor-current shim, and (re)apply the DBX revocation so the old binary can't load; reset boot order with efibootmgr. 3) Hunt: check UC3 for accompanying `mokutil --disable-validation`/SBAT reset, and scan other hosts for the same file hash and writing-process lineage.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/boot/efi/" or FolderPath has "/EFI/"
| where FileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","zypp","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub","packagekitd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has "/boot/efi/" or TargetFilePath has "/EFI/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("dpkg","rpm","apt","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Old Vulnerable Shim/GRUB EFI Binary Written to ESP by Non-Installer
id: 5c2f8a41-9b6e-4d13-8a77-2e1c4b90d6f2
description: Detects a shim/MokManager/GRUB EFI binary written into /boot/efi by a process that is not a legitimate package manager or firmware updater, consistent with staging an older Microsoft-signed vulnerable shim to bypass Secure Boot (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/
  - https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1542.003
  - attack.t1542.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/boot/efi/'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - 'shimx64.efi'
      - 'shimaa64.efi'
      - 'mmx64.efi'
      - 'grubx64.efi'
      - 'fbx64.efi'
      - 'bootx64.efi'
  filter_installer:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/apt'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/yum'
      - '/zypper'
      - '/fwupd'
      - '/grub-install'
      - '/grub2-install'
      - '/shim-install'
      - '/update-grub'
  condition: selection and not filter_installer
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/boot\/efi\/.*(shimx64|shimaa64|shimia32|mmx64|grubx64|fbx64|bootx64)\.efi$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|rpm|apt|apt-get|dnf|yum|zypper|fwupd|fwupdmgr|grub2?-install|shim-install|update-grub)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.file_name IN ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi") Endpoint.file_path="*/boot/efi/*" NOT Endpoint.process_name IN ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub") by Endpoint.dest, Endpoint.file_name, Endpoint.file_path, Endpoint.process_name, Endpoint.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.file_name IN ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi") Endpoint.file_path="*/boot/efi/*" NOT Endpoint.process_name IN ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub") by Endpoint.dest, Endpoint.file_name, Endpoint.file_path, Endpoint.process_name, Endpoint.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
MOK/SBAT enforcement disabled via mokutil (Secure Boot validation subversion) AIInstallation Medium
Detects mokutil invocations that disable shim signature validation or roll back the SBAT revocation policy — the exact levers the article describes for bypassing MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement so an older revoked shim will load unchallenged. Pairs with UC2 to catch the enforcement-weakening half of the chain. Rationale: The article states the bypass works by defeating MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement; `mokutil --disable-validation` and `--set-sbat-policy` (with `--import`/`--reset`) are the precise CLI levers to do that (corroborated by shim/mokutil docs). Named binary + dangerous flags keeps it targeted rather than a generic 'mokutil ran' dashboard. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1553.006 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin enrolling a new MOK for a third-party/DKMS driver (`mokutil --import`)
  • Sanctioned SBAT policy rollback during a distro-support troubleshooting case
  • NVIDIA/VirtualBox/DKMS module signing workflows on first install
  • Golden-image build pipelines enrolling keys before hardening
  • Lab/test hosts where an engineer disabled validation intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dkms","akmods","packagekitd") and ProcessCommandLine has "--import")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the invoking user/parent is an expected admin/automation account and whether a DKMS/third-party driver install is in flight; `--disable-validation` and SBAT `--reset` outside a change window are the red flags. 2) Contain: re-enable validation (`mokutil --enable-validation`), restore the current SBAT level, and revoke any unexpected enrolled MOK; isolate if paired with an ESP shim write (UC2). 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for a recent shim/GRUB EFI write (UC2), new efibootmgr boot-order changes, and reboots shortly after; sweep the fleet for the same command lineage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mokutil"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mokutil"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shim Signature Validation or SBAT Policy Disabled via mokutil
id: a1e7b4c9-3d20-4f8a-9c11-6b7e5f2a0d34
description: Detects mokutil disabling shim signature validation or resetting the SBAT revocation policy, weakening MOK-denylist/SBAT enforcement so an older revoked Microsoft-signed shim can load (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/
  - https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:

  - attack.t1562.001

    Image|endswith: '/mokutil'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--disable-validation'
      - '--set-sbat-policy'
      - '--import'
      - '--reset'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:mokutil OR @process.command_line:*mokutil*) @process.command_line:(*--disable-validation* OR *--set-sbat-policy* OR *--import* OR *--reset*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/mokutil$/i
| CommandLine=/(--disable-validation|--set-sbat-policy|--import|--reset)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.process_name="mokutil" (Endpoint.process="*--disable-validation*" OR Endpoint.process="*--set-sbat-policy*" OR Endpoint.process="*--import*" OR Endpoint.process="*--reset*") by Endpoint.dest, Endpoint.user, Endpoint.process_name, Endpoint.process, Endpoint.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
